title: How To Make A Warning Most Effective
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin reframes the classroom warning not as a consequence but as a courtesy, arguing that mislabeling it as a punishment undermines its purpose. A warning simply informs a student that a rule has been broken, with nothing further required of them, giving them a chance to self-correct before an actual consequence follows. He emphasizes that teachers should deliver warnings calmly and matter-of-factly and then walk away without waiting for a reaction, treating them as a one-way transfer of information and responsibility. Framed this way, warnings become easier for teachers to deliver without frustration and, over time, foster greater student maturity, independence, and willingness to self-correct without adult intervention.

quotes: In this way, it works like a consequence. It looks like a consequence. It acts like a consequence. It smells like a consequence. But in the truest sense, it isn’t a consequence. It’s a courtesy.
You see, other than being informed that they broke a class rule, nothing else happens to a student who first transgresses your rules.
Your only job is to inform, calmly and matter-of-factly— or even kindly and apologetically if the situation warrants—and then walk away without waiting for a response.
You no longer have to fret, sigh, harrumph, convince, coerce, question, glare, or otherwise make a show of your displeasure when a student misbehaves.
It becomes a simple courtesy you offer your students. An act of grace, trust, respect, and expectation that they will fix the problem.
